title: The fox and the fish (Berakhot 61b)
hookLine: Akiva's parable: fish in danger in the water would surely die on land
tomorrow: one short verse, and the whole Torah hangs on it. which one?
last: ALL GOD DOES IS FOR GOOD.

cards: Keep your head down for a while. Parents say it, friends say it, and often they're right. Now set it in the Talmud.

The Roman government has forbidden Jews to study Torah. Rabbi Akiva gathers crowds anyway, in public, teaching. A man named Pappos ben Yehuda finds him and asks: Akiva, aren't you afraid of the government?
Two people, both serious, and both have a case.

teach.b: Start with Pappos, because his question is a good one. A teacher who's arrested teaches no one.

And the Torah itself says of its laws that a person shall live by them; the sages read that line to mean live, and in most cases not die, for them. Pappos is asking Akiva to stay alive to teach another day.
Now Akiva's answer, a parable. A fox walks along a river and sees fish darting from place to place. What are you running from, he asks.
From the nets people cast for us, they say.

teach.h: THE FOX: COME UP ON LAND.
teach.b: So the fox says: come up onto dry land, and we'll live together, you and I, the way our ancestors did. And the fish answer: you're the one they call the cleverest of animals? You're a fool.
If we're afraid here, in the place that keeps us alive, how much more on land, where we'd surely die. Then Akiva explains.

Deuteronomy says it: "for that is thy life, and the length of thy days." If we're in danger while we study, how much more if we stop. Here's what to tell a friend tonight: the fox isn't offering danger.

He's offering safety, and the safety is the trap. The page ends hard, and gently said: soon both men are arrested, and Pappos, put beside Akiva, says happy are you, held for Torah, and woe to me, held for empty things.
The Talmud lets both speak. Pappos wanted Akiva alive. Akiva wanted to stay in the water.

how: The fox and the fish is told in Jewish schools and sermons as Akiva's answer to persecution; Akiva's death is remembered among the martyrs in the Yom Kippur prayers.

games.q: what does “the fox and the fish” mean?
o: a warning that study should stop when times get hard
Akiva's parable: fish leave the water to be safe, and die
a fable about a clever fox who outsmarts hungry fish

games.q: who says what — tap the pairs.
p: aren't you afraid of the government?

s: in the parable, the fox threatens the fish
he offers them safety on land. the safety is the trap.
the sages read 'live by them' to mean, in most cases, live and not die for the laws
that's the weight behind Pappos's question.
Pappos stays free and Akiva is arrested alone
both are arrested. Pappos says woe to him, held for empty things.

games.q: you have to argue Pappos's side in class. what's his strongest case?
o: a living teacher can teach tomorrow, and the Torah says live by its laws.
Torah study just isn't worth the trouble when times are hard.
the government is always right, so its law comes first.
games.why: Pappos isn't against Torah. he wants Akiva alive to teach it. Akiva answers that leaving the water is the bigger danger.

practice: Close your eyes and name your water: the one practice, place or people that keeps you most alive inside. Picture moving through it easily, the way a fish doesn't think about swimming.
Then notice one way you've been tempted onto dry land lately.

wordCard.voice: The fox and the fish. Akiva's parable for Pappos: leaving the water to be safe is how fish die.

orig.note: Hebrew: for that is thy life. Deuteronomy 30:20, the verse Akiva leans on.

carryVoice: Your line for today: water is our life, even when the water has nets in it. Forty-two of fifty.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 61b (Rome forbids Torah study; Pappos ben Yehuda's question; the fox and the fish; the arrests of Akiva and Pappos)
